sections.h2: Your options for selling in La Crosse
sections.html:
La Crosse homeowners can go with an agent, a private sale, or a cash buyer who accepts the house untouched. The estimated population of 50,784 on July 1, 2025 is down 3.6 percent from 52,691 in April 2020.

Your schedule and the state of the house usually settle the choice. Listing shows the property to the largest group of buyers, including people who work at the big local employers and the university. A direct sale is a better match for an owner who is moving, a vacant rental, an estate, or repairs you would rather not pay for.

Renting is common in La Crosse. Owners occupy just 46.1 percent of homes, so rentals dominate much of the market and many sellers are investors or heirs. The blocks around UW-La Crosse behave differently from the quieter residential streets, because many households there are students.

Jobs and campuses shape demand. Name the closest large employer or school in your description. Distance to the job is the first question those households ask, and answering it early saves a round of back-and-forth messages.

Values and incomes are modest, and the drive to work is short. A citywide middle figure is only a loose guide to one house.

Workers average 15.9 minutes to get to their jobs, a point worth raising with buyers.

Thirteen voting wards make up La Crosse, and its neighborhoods include Bluffside, Washburn, Historic Cass and King, Powell-Poage-Hamilton, Historic Downtown, Northside, Grandview Emerson, Weigent Hogan, Hintgen, College Park and Springbrook Clayton Johnson. College Park is the district around the University of Wisconsin-La Crosse campus. Use the neighborhood name in your listing so buyers who search by area can find you.

Roads include Interstate 90, U.S. 14, 53 and 61, and state highways 35, 16 and 33. Two bridges, on Cass Street and Cameron Avenue, link downtown with La Crescent, Minnesota, and La Crosse Regional Airport has scheduled flights to Chicago.

sections.h2: Rental rules that affect a La Crosse house
sections.html:
Both long-term and short-term rentals are regulated here, so an investor selling a rental house should know what applies. The Building and Inspections office, part of Planning and Development, registers residential rental units for $10 per parcel on its application (inspection@cityoflacrosse.org or 608-789-7530). Ask whether the registration stays with you or the buyer must register again.

Article XIX of the city code covers short-term rentals, meaning a residential dwelling rented for a fee for fewer than 30 consecutive days. The City Clerk issues the license. It cannot be handed to a buyer, and nobody may advertise until the county, state and local permits are in place, so anyone planning to run a short-term rental must apply on their own.

  • Rental unit registration: Building and Inspections.
  • Short-term rental license: City Clerk, under Article XIX.
  • Tax account questions: La Crosse County Treasurer, 212 6th Street North, (608) 785-9711, open 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays.

The transfer fee is the seller's cost: Wis. Stat. 77.22 sets it at 30 cents per $100 of value or fraction thereof, payable to the county register of deeds at recording. The electronic return is signed by both parties, and the register will not record a deed lacking it.

Some transfers owe nothing, including inheritance by will or descent and gifts from parent to child for nominal consideration (Wis. Stat. 77.25). Expect these steps:

  • Start title work and request a mortgage payoff letter.
  • Submit the transfer return to the Department of Revenue and save the receipt.
  • Have the La Crosse County Register of Deeds record the deed.
  • Pay prorated taxes at closing.

Once a buyer signs, write down the contract date, since it starts the 10-day clock for the condition report. After that, several tasks overlap. You handle title work and a payoff request, both sides sign the electronic transfer return, and a buyer who is borrowing arranges an inspection and financing.

Cash buyers typically close when title work finishes, while borrowers must wait for an appraisal and final loan approval. Either way, you finish by signing the deed, having it recorded with the return receipt, and settling your mortgage payoff and share of taxes from the proceeds.

sections.h2: Questions to settle before you accept an offer
sections.html:
Before you commit, write down answers to a few practical questions. Is a mortgage or lien attached, and what is the payoff figure? Does a rental registration exist for the parcel, and who will carry it after the sale? Are there bookings, tenants or a lease that run past the date you want to leave?

Next, look at taxes. The treasurer can tell you how much of this year's bill is paid and when the next installment falls. Lastly, decide which offers meet your timeline. An offer that closes on your day can beat a slightly bigger one that hinges on a lender.

sections.h2: If you own a rental or student house
sections.html:
If renters live in the house, check the lease end date and the tenant's notice rights before naming a closing day. Buyers who keep the tenants inherit the lease, and buyers who want the house empty must agree a date with the occupants. If the house has been a short-term rental, cancel stays booked beyond closing and let the buyer know the license does not follow the house.

Keep your rental registration, income records and repair receipts in one folder. Investors buying a rental ask for them first, and a cash buyer can often make a firm offer faster when they see the history.

The report asks what you know, so set aside an hour and walk through the house with the form. Check the basement for water marks, the roof for age, and the furnace and plumbing for repairs you remember.

Answer plainly and avoid guessing. A line marked "not aware" is acceptable when it is true. If something changes between acceptance and closing, tell the buyer in writing so the file stays accurate.

Sellers of a one-to-four unit property hand the buyer a finished Real Estate Condition Report within 10 days of accepting the contract. A late report gives the buyer two business days beyond day ten to rescind and get any deposit back (Wis. Stat. 709.02). Executors and trustees who never occupied the house are excused.

The real estate tax bill splits into two equal payments, due by January 31 and July 31, unless it totals under $100 (Wis. Stat. 74.11). Anything past due goes to the county treasurer, along with interest and penalties dating back to the previous February 1. The treasurer can quote the current balance ahead of your closing date, and the next payment falls on January 31, 2027.

faqs.q: How long does it take to sell a house in La Crosse?
faqs.a: Mostly it depends on the route. Selling on the market means tours, an inspection and a buyer's loan approval. A direct sale needs only completed title work and a filed return. Your title company can map out dates once a contract is signed.

faqs.q: Do I need a license to sell a La Crosse rental house?
faqs.a: Selling needs no license, but a rental unit is registered with Building and Inspections for $10 per parcel. A short-term rental license is issued by the City Clerk and stays with you, so the buyer must apply anew.

faqs.q: What does the transfer fee cost in La Crosse?
faqs.a: Sellers pay 30 cents on each $100 of value, and a leftover fraction counts as another $100. The county register of deeds takes the payment when it records the deed.

faqs.q: Where do I pay property tax in La Crosse?
faqs.a: Money paid through January 31 goes to the local taxation district treasurer. After that date, pay the county treasurer at 212 6th Street North, phone (608) 785-9711.

faqs.q: Can an estate sell a La Crosse house without a condition report?
faqs.a: Yes, if the fiduciary never lived there: chapter 709 excuses a personal representative, trustee or court-appointed fiduciary. A deed, a transfer return and any exemption wording the register wants are still needed.
